explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve that emerges from the posterior aspect of the brainstem, specifically from the dorsal surface of the midbrain.
The cisterna magna (cerebellomedullary cistern) is the largest subarachnoid cistern located between the cerebellum and the medulla oblongata.
The spinocerebellum (vermis and intermediate hemisphere) regulates muscle tone and coordination; the neocerebellum plans movement and the paleocerebellum controls equilibrium.
Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome) results from PICA infarction, causing ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ataxia, and hoarseness.
Inferior pons lesion affecting CN VI nucleus causes facial weakness (CN VII) and lateral rectus weakness (CN VI), with normal sensation pointing to a pontine tumor.
Intention tremor, overshoot (dysmetria), and swaying to the right during gait indicate a right cerebellar lesion; the tumor is in the right cerebellum.
Syringomyelia damages the crossing spinothalamic fibers in the cervical cord, causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature with preserved tactile discrimination.
Bilateral gracile tract degeneration in tabes dorsalis causes loss of proprioception leading to sensory ataxia with positive Romberg sign (swaying with eyes closed).
Chorea (jerky, non-purposeful movements) with hypotonia results from caudate nucleus degeneration in Huntington disease, an autosomal dominant condition.
Glioblastoma multiforme typically crosses the corpus callosum (butterfly glioma), shows necrosis and ring enhancement, and has poor prognosis.
A biconvex, lens-shaped hyperdensity between skull and dura is an epidural hematoma, typically from traumatic middle meningeal artery rupture.
First pharyngeal arch derivatives include mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bone, and muscles of mastication; defect causes Treacher Collins-like features.
Pilocytic astrocytoma in children shows characteristic hair-like processes (ROSE), microcysts, and Rosenthal fibers; often cystic with mural nodule.
Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) at cerebellopontine angle shows Antoni A (cellular) and Antoni B (hypocellular) areas with verocay bodies.
Medulloblastoma shows loss of chromosome 17p; it's a small round blue cell tumor of the posterior fossa in children.
Multiple sclerosis shows perivascular lymphocytic cuffing with demyelinated axons in white matter and oligoclonal IgG bands in CSF.
Ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm, associated with polycystic kidney disease and autosomal dominant inheritance, is the most common cause of spontaneous SAH.
Multiple sclerosis presents with oligoclonal bands in CSF, periventricular white matter lesions, and relapsing-remitting neurological deficits.
The lamina terminalis forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle; it is a thin membrane derived from the telencephalon containing the organum vasculosum.
The mandibular nerve (V3) runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus floor, not the lateral wall; oculomotor, trochlear, V1, and V2 are in the lateral wall.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) emerges from the anterior aspect of the medulla between the pyramid and olive, carrying only motor fibers.
Internal arcuate fibers are axons of the cuneate and gracile nuclei that cross at the sensory decussation to form the medial lemniscus.
The cuneate tract carries proprioception from the upper limb (including biceps brachii) and synapses in the cuneate nucleus of the medulla.
The spinotectal tract carries pain information to the superior colliculus for reflex head and eye movements toward cutaneous stimuli.
The trigeminal nerve does not wind around the cerebral peduncle; optic tract, trochlear nerve, posterior cerebral artery, and basal vein do.
The central tegmental tract (carrying pallidal and cerebellar projections) is present at midbrain level, running between red nucleus and inferior olivary nucleus.
The facial colliculus on the floor of the fourth ventricle is formed by the abducens nucleus, around which the facial nerve fibers loop.
The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle is located in the inferior roof (posterior medullary velum), not the floor or superior roof.
The intermaxillary segment (from medial nasal prominences) forms the philtrum of the upper lip, the primary palate, and the four incisor teeth.
The lateral upper lip derives from the maxillary prominence (branchial arch 1), along with the lateral cheek and most of the upper lip.
First pharyngeal arch defect (Treacher Collins syndrome) causes underdeveloped mandible, zygomatic bones, and low-set ears.
Tensor veli palatini develops from the first pharyngeal arch, innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies the third branchial arch, which gives rise to stylopharyngeus muscle and the stylotympanic fissure.
Meissner corpuscles in the dermal papillae detect fine touch, texture, and two-point discrimination; they adapt rapidly and are numerous in fingertips.
Meissner corpuscles detect fine tactile details and edges, enabling blind individuals to read Braille through subtle texture differences.
